chunks: As for what Sahl ibn Ziyad narrated from Ibn Mahbub, from Yunus ibn Ya'qub, who said:

When Abu al-Hasan Musa (peace be upon him) was returning from Baghdad and proceeding to Medina, a daughter of his died at Fayd. He buried her and ordered some of his mawali to plaster her grave, to write her name on a tablet, and to place it in the grave.

The correct interpretation of this narration is that it lifts the prohibition against doing that and constitutes a form of dispensation (rukhsa), because the first narration was delivered in the context of dislike (karaha/makruh), not prohibition (hazr).

key_terms.الرُّخْصَةِ: rukhsa — a jurisprudential dispensation permitting what is otherwise discouraged
key_terms.الْحَظْرِ: hazr — absolute prohibition, the stricter jurisprudential grade
key_terms.الْكَرَاهَةِ: karaha — the fiqh grade of 'dislike' or makruh, less severe than outright prohibition
key_terms.يُجَصِّصَ: to plaster with gypsum (tajsis) — the act whose legal status is under scrutiny

ai.seo_question: What did Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS) order regarding his daughter's grave at Fayd, and what legal ruling does this establish in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith records that Imam Musa al-Kazim (AS), while traveling from Baghdad toward Medina, buried his daughter who died at Fayd and ordered his mawali to plaster her grave and place a name-inscribed tablet in it. Sheikh al-Tusi appends jurisprudential commentary explaining that the Imam's action constitutes a rukhsa (dispensation) reconciling the earlier prohibitive narration in the chapter: grave plastering falls under karaha (reprehensibility/makruh) rather than outright hazr (prohibition).
